NeuroVLM · internal evaluation report

MLP vs. Atlas-Free CNN

Head-to-head comparison of the packaged NeuroVLM MLP baseline against the atlas-free 3D CNN branch, across three capabilities and three datasets.

DatasetsPubMed · Nilearn · NeuroVault
CapabilitiesAE reconstruction · contrastive retrieval · text-to-brain generation
Models compared1 MLP · 16 CNN variants
Sourceexperiments/3dcnn/atlas_free_cnn/evaluation

Key findings

The short version, before the per-capability detail below.

Stage 1 · reconstruction

CNN wins outside PubMed

On PubMed, MLP and CNN reconstruct about equally well (spatial corr 0.804 vs. best CNN 0.776). On NeuroVault the gap is large: MLP 0.275 vs. CNN 0.895 — expected, since the MLP was never trained on continuous NeuroVault-style maps.

Stage 3 · retrieval

Domain-matched CNN dominates

The CNN branch trained/evaluated on its own domain leads everywhere except PubMed, where MLP is competitive (83% bidirectional AUC). On NeuroVault, CNN mixed-baseline reaches 85% vs. MLP's 47%.

Stage 4 · generation

MLP still ahead on PubMed text-to-brain

MLP leads generation quality on PubMed (r−random 0.168 vs. best CNN 0.069), but has no supported path on Nilearn at all, and trails CNN on NeuroVault (0.037 vs. 0.087).

Shared setup

What both model families are, where the data comes from, and how a model trained on one modality gets evaluated against another.

The two model families

MLP (mlp_neurovlm) is the packaged NeuroVLM baseline on main: a NeuroAutoEncoder (28,542-voxel masker-flat space, MNI152 4mm) plus Hugging Face projection heads, loaded via src/neurovlm/retrieval_resources.py. It was trained on binary PubMed activation masks.

Atlas-free CNN is a 3D CNN operating on (36, 45, 38) ALE-style volumes, also on the MNI152 4mm grid but cropped to the brain bounding box. It comes in a mixed branch (pretrained across all three domains) and three domain-specialized branches (fine-tuned separately on PubMed, Nilearn, or NeuroVault).

The masker-crop bridge

The MLP's masker and the atlas-free CNN's volumes turn out to occupy the exact same MNI152 4mm grid: the CNN's (36, 45, 38) volumes are literally the MLP mask's own brain-bounding-box crop (verified directly — the crop contains exactly 28,542 voxels, matching the MLP masker's voxel count, with an identical affine). That means a CNN volume converts to MLP masker-flat space with a single boolean index, no resampling — implemented in mlp_masker_bridge.py. This is what makes an MLP-vs-CNN comparison possible on Nilearn and NeuroVault at all, since neither has a native flat resource in the main package the way PubMed does.

Because the MLP encoder was trained on binary masks, continuous Nilearn/NeuroVault maps are binarized (x > 0) before encoding — the same convention already used for MLP evaluation in docs/03_evaluation/11_autoencoder.ipynb and 12_neurovault_decoding.ipynb.

Data provenance

All three comparisons read from the same held-out unified test split (3,347 rows: 3,066 PubMed, 202 NeuroVault, 75 Nilearn across 8 atlas sources), pulled from neurovlm/atlas_free_cnn_dataset on Hugging Face with local-cache-first resolution. Text is embedded with the normalized SPECTER2 cache (specter2_stage3_stage4_emptycentered_unitnorm.pt + its metadata/validation/index sidecars), same repo, same local-first/HF-fallback pattern. For Nilearn contrastive retrieval specifically, MLP has no precomputed text embedding at all, so text is embedded on the fly with the same SPECTER2 model+adapter (allenai/specter2_aug2023refresh, adhoc_query) used to build the MLP's own PubMed/NeuroVault text latents, rather than the CNN's differently-preprocessed cache.

Numbers in this report come from --limit-capped runs (16 AE samples, 32 retrieval pairs, 8 generation samples per dataset/model) — enough to see clear separation between models, not a claim of final statistical power. See Limitations.

STAGE 1

Autoencoder reconstruction

Can each model encode a brain map to a latent and decode it back out again?

How it was set up

Script: atlas_free_cnn.evaluation.compare_ae_reconstruction. For each dataset/model pair, a batch of held-out volumes is encoded then decoded, and the reconstruction is scored against the (possibly binarized) target in a shared metric space:

  • PubMed · MLP — uses the main package's dedicated flat resource (load_dataset("pubmed_images")), which is already binary. Comparison space: mlp_masker_flatmap.
  • Nilearn / NeuroVault · MLP — the atlas-free CNN's test volumes are binarized, converted to MLP masker-flat space via the crop bridge, encoded/decoded by the MLP autoencoder, then converted back to volume space so metrics are computed the same way as the CNN's. Comparison space: atlas_free_volume_via_mlp_masker_crop.
  • All datasets · CNN — native 3D volumes in, native 3D volumes out. Comparison space: native_atlas_free_volume.

Metrics (via generation_metrics): spatial correlation (global Pearson r over all in-mask voxels), top-5% Dice (overlap of the top 5% highest-value voxels in prediction vs. target), foreground MSE (MSE restricted to nonzero target voxels), and voxel AUROC (ranking predicted intensity against a top-5th-percentile target threshold).

Reading this: on PubMed the two families are close (MLP's own training domain). On NeuroVault and Nilearn, CNN reconstructs substantially better on spatial correlation and Dice — unsurprising, since MLP is reconstructing through a binary-mask encoder it was never trained for. MLP's voxel AUROC stays high everywhere (0.95–0.99) because AUROC is a ranking metric within each sample and tolerant of the miscalibrated intensity scale that hurts MSE/Dice.
STAGE 3

Contrastive retrieval

Given a piece of text, can the model rank the matching brain map above the rest of the batch — and the reverse?

How it was set up

Script: atlas_free_cnn.evaluation.compare_contrastive_retrieval. Each model embeds both a batch of texts and a batch of brain maps into its own shared space, then retrieval is scored in both directions:

  • PubMed · MLP — official PubMed test-split images + SPECTER2 text latents, run through the MLP autoencoder encoder and InfoNCE projection heads.
  • NeuroVault · MLP — main-package NeuroVault images, binarized, same encoder/projection path.
  • Nilearn · MLP — atlas-free CNN test volumes via the masker-crop bridge (binarized), paired with on-the-fly SPECTER2 embeddings of the Nilearn atlas-region text (see Shared setup).
  • CNN — the matching Stage 3 checkpoint's brain encoder + text projection, evaluated on the atlas-free unified test split. cnn_contrastive_mixed resolves per-dataset to the mixed-pretrained encoder evaluated on that domain (mixed_to_pubmed / _to_nilearn / _to_neurovault); the domain-specialized checkpoints (cnn_contrastive_pubmed, etc.) are fixed and evaluated on all three datasets, in-domain or out.

Metric: normalized Recall@K AUC (neurovlm.retrieval_metrics.bidirectional_retrieval_metrics) — area under the recall-vs-normalized-K curve, 0.5 at chance, 1.0 for perfect ranking — reported bidirectionally (Text-to-Brain, Brain-to-Text) and as their mean, plus MRR.

Recall@K curves

Reading this: a domain-specialized or mixed-baseline CNN checkpoint evaluated in its own domain is the strongest performer everywhere. MLP is competitive on PubMed (83% bidirectional AUC, second only to the in-domain CNN) but falls toward chance-adjacent territory on NeuroVault (47%) — the domain gap seen in Stage 1 shows up here too. Cross-domain CNN checkpoints (e.g. a PubMed-specialized encoder evaluated on Nilearn) consistently underperform the domain-matched one, which is the expected direction for a real specialization effect rather than a leaderboard artifact.
STAGE 4

Text-to-brain generation

Given text alone, generate a brain map and compare it against the real one.

How it was set up

Script: atlas_free_cnn.evaluation.compare_text_to_brain_generation. Text goes in, a full brain map comes out, and that generated map is scored against the ground truth:

  • PubMed · MLP — official test-split abstracts through NeuroVLM.text(...).to_brain(head="mse"), scored against the paper's true PubMed image.
  • NeuroVault · MLP — publication text through the same generation path, matched against the best of that publication's candidate NeuroVault images (precomputed latents, existing evaluation_notebook_utils.build_neurovault_t2b_eval path).
  • Nilearn · MLP — not supported. Text-to-brain generation additionally requires a paired ground-truth image and the MLP's own generation head; no such resource exists for Nilearn in the main package, and (unlike Stages 1/3) the masker-crop bridge alone doesn't supply a generation target for this direction. Reported as a skipped row, not a zero.
  • CNN — the matching Stage 4 projector + domain autoencoder decoder generates a volume from a SPECTER2 embedding; scored natively in atlas-free volume space, plus via a Stage 3 evaluator projecting the generated volume back into shared contrastive space for a retrieval-style check.

Metrics: Pearson r and Spearman ρ against a per-dataset/family random voxel-subset baseline (so a raw r of 0.1 that beats a ~0.0 random baseline reads differently from one that doesn't), Dice at the 90th percentile (plus a full 80–95th percentile sensitivity curve), voxel AUROC, native generation_metrics (spatial corr / foreground MSE / top-K Dice), and generated-image–to-text retrieval AUC.

Per-sample spread

Dice sensitivity

Reading this: MLP leads PubMed generation quality (r−random 0.168 vs. best CNN 0.069) — its strongest showing across all three stages, consistent with PubMed being its native training domain end-to-end (encoder and generation head). On NeuroVault the CNN mixed/specialized branches edge ahead (0.087 vs. MLP's 0.037), and Nilearn has no MLP result to compare at all.

Limitations & known gaps

  • Sample sizes are small by design. 16 / 32 / 8 samples per dataset–model cell (Stages 1/3/4) are enough to see separation, not enough for tight confidence intervals — treat single-decimal differences as directional, not conclusive.
  • Spin significance testing was disabled (--skip-spin) for the Stage 4 run behind this report, for turnaround time. The Dice-sensitivity and per-sample panels still hold, but no spin-test p-values are reported here.
  • MLP has three real (not workaround-able) coverage gaps: no text-to-brain generation on Nilearn (no paired ground-truth resource), and Stages 1 and 3 on Nilearn/NeuroVault only exist because of the masker-crop bridge — a genuine, verified equivalence, but still a bridge rather than a resource the MLP was built for.
  • Nilearn itself is a small, heterogeneous domain — 75 held-out rows spanning 8 different atlas types (BASC, DiFuMo, Harvard-Oxford, Juelich, MSDL, Schaefer, Smith, Yeo), each with its own statistical character. Nilearn numbers should be read as "this domain is hard and sparse for everyone," not just "for the MLP."
